questions.text: What is the defining feature of a price-taking firm?

options.a: It faces market demand as a perfectly inelastic line.
options.b: It can raise market price by restricting output alone.
options.c: It chooses the market price and sells any output it wants.
options.d: It treats the market output price as unaffected by its own production decision.

questions.text: Which market structure is most consistent with perfect competition?

options.a: Several firms colluding to choose a common price.
options.b: A sole buyer of labor with upward-sloping input supply.
options.c: One firm selling a unique product with no close substitutes.
options.d: Many small firms selling a homogeneous good with negligible individual market power.

questions.text: How does the demand curve facing an individual price-taking firm appear at a given market price?

options.a: Vertical at its profit-maximizing output.
options.b: Horizontal at the market price.
options.c: The same downward-sloping curve as market demand.
options.d: Upward sloping through the origin.

questions.text: Why is it incorrect to confuse the demand facing one competitive firm with total market demand?

options.a: One firm can sell at a given price without materially affecting it, while total market quantity affects market equilibrium price.
options.b: Both must be perfectly horizontal.
options.c: The market demand includes only this firm's output.
options.d: Both must be vertical.

questions.text: What is marginal revenue for a price-taking firm?

options.a: Market price.
options.b: Zero at every level of production.
options.c: Average variable cost.
options.d: Market price minus marginal cost.

questions.text: Why does a competitive firm choose quantity rather than independently set price?

options.a: At the market price, it faces a perfectly elastic residual demand under the model's assumptions.
options.b: It has a perfectly inelastic demand curve.
options.c: It has no control over its technology.
options.d: It can never shut down.

questions.text: What is the standard interior first-order condition for a competitive firm's optimal output?

options.a: Price equals marginal revenue minus marginal cost.
options.b: Price equals marginal cost.
options.c: Total revenue equals total variable cost.
options.d: Price equals average fixed cost.

questions.text: Why is the condition p=MC not sufficient by itself for the global profit-maximizing output?

options.a: Marginal cost must be negative.
options.b: One must also check that output is on the relevant rising MC branch and that producing is better than shutting down.
options.c: Price must equal total cost rather than marginal cost.
options.d: A competitive firm always operates at zero output.

questions.text: What is the relevant second-order condition for a smooth interior competitive supply optimum?

options.a: Average fixed cost is increasing.
options.b: Market demand has elasticity zero.
options.c: Marginal cost is locally nondecreasing with output.
options.d: Marginal cost is strictly negative.

questions.text: Which portion of marginal cost is the firm's short-run supply curve under standard assumptions?

options.a: The upward-sloping MC portion at or above minimum average variable cost.
options.b: The average fixed cost curve.
options.c: The entire MC curve, including points below minimum AVC.
options.d: The average total cost curve.

questions.text: Why can a competitive firm with p less than AC still rationally produce in the short run?

options.a: Profit maximization requires p greater than AC at every output.
options.b: Revenue may cover variable costs and contribute toward unavoidable fixed costs.
options.c: It necessarily earns positive accounting profit.
options.d: Fixed costs disappear when output is positive.

questions.text: What is the short-run shutdown rule for a competitive firm with avoidable variable costs?

options.a: Shut down when price is below minimum AVC.
options.b: Always produce whenever price is positive.
options.c: Shut down when price exceeds MC.
options.d: Shut down whenever price is below AC.

questions.text: At a market price equal to the minimum average variable cost, what can be true?

options.a: The firm must supply an infinite amount.
options.b: The firm must have negative variable costs.
options.c: The firm can be indifferent between operating at the shutdown output and producing zero, ignoring other complications.
options.d: The firm must make positive economic profit.

questions.text: If price is below minimum average variable cost, why is producing worse than temporarily shutting down?

options.a: Operating revenue does not cover the variable cost of any positive production plan.
options.b: Marginal revenue is negative for a competitive firm.
options.c: Average total cost is always below price.
options.d: All fixed costs can be avoided by shutting down.

questions.text: What cost must a firm pay in the usual short-run model even if it produces zero?

options.a: Variable production cost for positive output.
options.b: Producer surplus.
options.c: Marginal cost of the last unit.
options.d: Unavoidable fixed cost.

questions.text: How is the competitive firm's inverse supply described on its active short-run supply branch?

options.a: Price equals marginal cost as a function of output.
options.b: Price equals total revenue minus fixed cost.
options.c: Price equals the derivative of consumer utility.
options.d: Price equals average fixed cost at all quantities.

questions.text: If market price rises along a competitive firm's active supply curve with rising MC, what happens to optimal output?

options.a: It falls.
options.b: It becomes negative.
options.c: It rises.
options.d: It remains strictly fixed.

questions.text: What happens if price is between minimum AVC and minimum AC for a competitive firm?

options.a: It may operate with a loss smaller than its unavoidable fixed cost.
options.b: It must shut down because it makes a loss.
options.c: It must produce zero because MR is negative.
options.d: It always earns positive economic profit.

questions.text: What is the crucial distinction between shutdown and exit?

options.a: Shutdown and exit are identical in every time horizon.
options.b: Exit means operating where price is below AVC.
options.c: Shutdown raises market price by fiat.
options.d: Shutdown is a short-run zero-output choice with unavoidable fixed costs; exit is a long-run decision that avoids all relevant costs.

questions.text: For a firm with output y and variable cost cv(y), how is producer surplus measured?

options.a: Variable cost minus total revenue.
options.b: p y - cv(y) - fixed cost.
options.c: p y - cv(y).
options.d: p y - fixed cost only.

questions.text: How are producer surplus and short-run economic profit related with fixed cost F?

options.a: Profit equals producer surplus plus fixed cost.
options.b: Profit equals producer surplus minus fixed cost.
options.c: Profit is the negative of producer surplus.
options.d: Profit always equals producer surplus for positive fixed cost.

questions.text: Under a continuous upward-sloping active supply schedule, how is producer surplus represented geometrically?

options.a: The area above demand and below price.
options.b: The area above the supply curve and below price up to the produced quantity.
options.c: Total expenditure on inputs including fixed cost.
options.d: The area to the right of market quantity only.

questions.text: If market price increases and a competitive firm adjusts output optimally, what happens to producer surplus?

options.a: It necessarily decreases.
options.b: It stays constant at all prices.
options.c: It weakly increases, holding costs and technology fixed.
options.d: It becomes equal to fixed cost.

questions.text: If fixed cost is unchanged, what is the relation between changes in short-run profit and producer surplus?

options.a: They always have opposite signs.
options.b: They are equal.
options.c: Producer surplus remains constant when profit changes.
options.d: They differ by twice the fixed cost.

questions.text: Can producer surplus be positive while economic profit is negative?

options.a: No, the two measures always have the same sign.
options.b: Yes, when positive producer surplus does not cover fixed cost.
options.c: Yes, but only if the product price is negative.
options.d: No, profit excludes fixed cost in economics.

questions.text: What does the vertical distance between price and AVC at produced output measure when multiplied by output?

options.a: Fixed cost.
options.b: Producer surplus.
options.c: Total cost.
options.d: Marginal revenue.

questions.text: What additional adjustments can a firm make in the long run relative to the short run?

options.a: It can ignore economic costs.
options.b: It can unilaterally determine the competitive market price.
options.c: It can alter fixed factors such as plant size.
options.d: It can choose consumer preferences.

questions.text: What is the basic long-run operating condition for positive production?

options.a: Price must be below marginal cost.
options.b: Price must equal average fixed cost.
options.c: Price must cover long-run average cost at the chosen scale.
options.d: Price may remain below every attainable long-run average cost indefinitely.

questions.text: What is the long-run break-even price for a firm with U-shaped long-run average cost and free exit?

options.a: The minimum of average fixed cost.
options.b: The maximum of marginal cost.
options.c: Zero regardless of technology.
options.d: The minimum of long-run average cost.

questions.text: What characterizes the long-run supply curve of a constant-returns-to-scale firm at the minimum unit cost cmin?

options.a: A downward-sloping curve with positive monopoly markup.
options.b: An upward-sloping curve through the origin at all quantities.
options.c: A strictly vertical supply curve.
options.d: A horizontal supply relationship at price cmin, with zero economic profit at feasible positive scales.

questions.text: Why is a firm's long-run supply generally more elastic than short-run supply?

options.a: More factors can adjust to price changes.
options.b: Long-run marginal cost must be zero.
options.c: The long-run output price is always lower.
options.d: Variable inputs become fixed in the long run.

questions.text: At the output where the chosen short-run plant size is also long-run optimal, what holds for marginal costs under differentiability?

options.a: Both must be negative.
options.b: Long-run marginal cost always exceeds short-run marginal cost.
options.c: Short-run and long-run marginal costs coincide.
options.d: Short-run marginal cost is zero.

questions.text: Why does perfect competition imply price equals marginal revenue for a firm but not for a monopoly?

options.a: A competitive firm has fixed total revenue.
options.b: A monopoly's marginal revenue always equals price.
options.c: A competitive firm takes market price as given when changing output, whereas a monopoly faces downward-sloping demand.
options.d: A monopoly has no production costs.

questions.text: If minimum AVC is €8 and minimum AC is €12, and the competitive price is €10, what is generally optimal?

options.a: Produce zero because price is below AC.
options.b: Exit immediately because short-run profits are negative.
options.c: Earn positive profit because price exceeds AVC.
options.d: Produce on the appropriate MC branch but earn a short-run economic loss.

questions.text: At price above minimum AC, what is possible for a price-taking firm operating at its optimum?

options.a: Variable costs exceed total revenue at every output.
options.b: A forced short-run shutdown.
options.c: Marginal revenue is negative.
options.d: Positive economic profit in the short run.

questions.text: What is the short-run supply response to a rise in fixed cost, holding variable costs and market price fixed?

options.a: The supply curve shifts upward by the fixed cost at every output.
options.b: The active MC supply schedule is unchanged, although profit falls.
options.c: Marginal revenue falls by the fixed cost.
options.d: Output must rise at every price.

questions.text: Why are technology and cost constraints relevant to competitive supply?

options.a: They make the firm's demand curve downward sloping.
options.b: They determine consumer income and preferences only.
options.c: They allow the firm to manipulate market price.
options.d: They determine MC and the cost-covering threshold at which supply is profitable to undertake.

questions.text: Why can the individual competitive firm's demand be horizontal even if the industry demand slopes downward?

options.a: The industry has only one buyer.
options.b: Industry quantities never affect equilibrium price.
options.c: The firm is small relative to the market and regards the market price as given.
options.d: Each firm sells a differentiated good at a chosen price.

questions.text: Why might a short-run competitive firm's profit-maximizing output be zero even at positive price?

options.a: Positive prices are impossible under competition.
options.b: Market demand is perfectly vertical.
options.c: A firm's MC is always below zero.
options.d: Price may be insufficient to cover any positive output's variable cost.

questions.text: According to the illustrated short-run cost curves, which part of MC is relevant for positive competitive supply?

options.a: The upward-sloping section above the shutdown threshold at minimum AVC.
options.b: Only the portion of MC below AVC.
options.c: The entire average fixed cost curve.
options.d: Every point on MC even below minimum AVC.
